scenes.heading: Energy from food
scenes.sub: Where do the kilojoules on a food label come from?
scenes.say: Every food label in Australia lists energy in kilojoules. That number comes from chemistry: the energy released when food molecules are oxidised to carbon dioxide and water.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A fully charged phone has more to give than a half-used one
scenes.science: Fats are less oxidised than sugars, so they release more energy
scenes.breaks: a battery stores energy in one device; food energy comes from bond energy differences when it reacts with oxygen.
scenes.say: Glucose already has about one oxygen per carbon, so it's partly oxidised, like a half-used phone battery. Fats are mostly carbon and hydrogen with very little oxygen, like a full battery. So each gram of fat has more reacting left to do.

scenes.heading: Energy values: 16, 17, 37
points: Fibre: little energy (we can't digest it)
scenes.say: Remember sixteen, seventeen, thirty-seven. Carbohydrate gives sixteen kilojoules per gram, protein seventeen, and fats and oils thirty-seven, more than double. Fibre gives little energy, because we can't digest it.
scenes.caption: Remember 16, 17, 37. Carbohydrate gives 16 kJ g⁻¹, protein 17, and fats and oils 37, more than double. Fibre gives little energy, because we can't digest it.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: A muesli bar has 18 g carbohydrate, 4.0 g protein and 6.0 g fat. Find its energy content.
scenes.say: Multiply each mass by its energy value. Carbohydrate gives two hundred and eighty-eight kilojoules, protein sixty-eight, and fat two hundred and twenty-two. The total is about five hundred and eighty kilojoules. Fat is a small part of the mass, but almost forty percent of the energy.
scenes.caption: Multiply each mass by its energy value. Carbohydrate gives 288 kJ, protein 68, and fat 222. The total is about 5.8 × 10² kJ. Fat is a small part of the mass, but almost 40% of the energy.

scenes.heading: Same equation, different road
scenes.say: Burning glucose and respiring it have the same overall equation and the same delta H. Combustion pays the bill in one huge burst. Respiration pays in small instalments, using enzymes at body temperature, so some energy is captured in ATP.
scenes.caption: Burning glucose and respiring it have the same overall equation and the same ΔH. Combustion pays the bill in one huge burst. Respiration pays in small instalments, using enzymes at body temperature, so some energy is captured in ATP.

scenes.heading: Glycaemic index (GI)
points: Ranks carbs by how fast blood glucose rises
Low: 55 or less; high: 70 or more
scenes.say: The glycaemic index ranks carbohydrate foods by how quickly they raise blood glucose, compared with glucose at one hundred. Low GI is fifty-five or less; high is seventy or more. Branched amylopectin is digested fast, while tightly coiled amylose is slower.
scenes.caption: The glycaemic index ranks carbohydrate foods by how quickly they raise blood glucose, compared with glucose at 100. Low GI is 55 or less; high is 70 or more. Branched amylopectin is digested fast, while tightly coiled amylose is slower.

scenes.heading: Measuring energy accurately
steps: Burn the food in the calorimeter
scenes.say: For accurate results, calibrate a bomb calorimeter first. Pass a known electrical energy, V I t, and find the calibration factor. Burn the food, and the energy is CF times delta T. A nut burned under a can gives a result that's far too low.
scenes.caption: For accurate results, calibrate a bomb calorimeter first. Pass a known electrical energy, VIt, and find the calibration factor. Burn the food, and the energy is CF × ΔT. A nut burned under a can gives a result that's far too low.

points: Fats are less oxidised, so more energy
Respiration: same ΔH, many small steps
GI is about speed, not kilojoules
q = mcΔT, or q = CF × ΔT
scenes.say: Quick recap. Sixteen, seventeen, thirty-seven. Fats release more because they're less oxidised. Respiration is controlled, step-by-step combustion. And GI is about speed, not kilojoules. Now try the practice questions!
